section.heading: 15.8. Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates
section.paragraph: Another useful coordinate system in three dimensions is the spherical coordinate system. It simplifies the evaluation of triple integrals over regions bounded by spheres or cones.
section.heading: Spherical Coordinates
section.paragraph: The spherical coordinates $$\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)$$ of a point $$P$$ in space are shown in Figure 1, where $$\rho = {|{OP}|}$$ is the distance from the origin to $$P$$ , $$\theta$$ is the same angle as in cylindrical coordinates, and $$\phi$$ is the angle between the positive $$z$$ -axis and the line segment $$OP$$ . Note that
$${\rho \geqslant 0} {0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi}$$

figure.caption: The spherical coordinates of a point

section.paragraph: The spherical coordinate system is especially useful in problems where there is symmetry about a point, and the origin is placed at this point. For example, the sphere with center the origin and radius $$c$$ has the simple equation $$\rho = c$$ (see Figure 2): this is the reason for the name “spherical” coordinates. The graph of the equation $$\theta = c$$ is a vertical half-plane (see Figure 3), and the equation $$\phi = c$$ represents a half-cone with the $$z$$ -axis as its axis (see Figure 4).

$${z = \rho\cos\phi} {r = \rho\sin\phi}$$

section.paragraph: But $$x = r\cos\theta$$ and $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , so to convert from spherical to rectangular coordinates, we use the equations
$${x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta} {y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta} {z = \rho\cos\phi}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The point $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 4,\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ is given in spherical coordinates. Plot the point and find its rectangular coordinates.
Solution We plot the point in Figure 6. From Equations 1 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}} \\ {y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}} \\ {z = \rho\cos\phi = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 2\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = 1} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A point and three lines segments are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. A line segment labeled 2 begins at the origin, slopes upward to the right at an angle pi/3from the positive z axis and ends at a point labeled (2, pi/4, pi/3). From this point, a vertical line segment descends downward to meet the x y plane. From here, a line segment on the x y plane reaches the origin and is at an angle pi/4 from the positive x axis.

example.paragraph: Thus the point $$({2,\pi \slash 4,\pi \slash 3})$$ is $$({\sqrt{3 \slash 2},\sqrt{3 \slash 2},1})$$ in rectangular coordinates.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: The point $$({0,2\sqrt{3}, - 2})$$ is given in rectangular coordinates. Find spherical coordinates for this point.
Solution From Equation 2 we have $$\rho = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} = \sqrt{0 + 12 + 4} = 4$$ and so Equations 1 give
$$\begin{array}{ll} {\cos\phi = \frac{z}{\rho} = \frac{- 2}{4} = - \frac{1}{2}} & { \phi = \frac{2\pi}{3}} \\ {\cos\theta = \frac{x}{\rho\sin\phi} = 0} & { \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$
(Note that $$\theta \neq 3\pi \slash 2$$ because $$y = 2\sqrt{3} > 0$$ .) Therefore spherical coordinates of the given point are $$\left( {4,\pi \slash 2,2\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ .
Warning There is not universal agreement on the notation for spherical coordinates. Most books on physics reverse the meanings of $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ and use $$r$$ in place of $$\rho$$ .

section.heading: Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates
section.paragraph: In the spherical coordinate system the counterpart of a rectangular box is a spherical wedge
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)|a \leqslant \rho \leqslant b,\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta,c \leqslant \phi \leqslant d} \right\}$$

where $$a \geqslant 0$$ and $$\beta - \alpha \leqslant 2\pi$$ , and $$d - c \leqslant \pi$$ . Although we defined triple integrals by dividing solids into small boxes, it can be shown that dividing a solid into small spherical wedges always gives the same result. So we divide $$E$$ into smaller spherical wedges $$E_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ by means of equally spaced spheres $$\rho = \rho_{i}$$ , half-planes $$\theta = \theta_{j}$$ , and half-cones $$\phi = \phi_{k}$$ . Figure 7 shows that $$E_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ is approximately a rectangular box with dimensions $$\Delta\rho$$ , $$\rho_{i}\Delta\phi$$ (arc of a circle with radius $$\rho_{i}$$ , angle $$\Delta\phi$$ ), and $$\rho_{i}\sin\phi_{k}\Delta\theta$$ (arc of a circle with radius $$\rho_{i}\sin\phi_{k}$$ , angle $$\Delta\theta$$ ). So an approximation to the volume of $$E_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ is given by

$$\Delta V_{\mathit{ijk}} \approx \left( {\Delta\rho} \right)\left( {\rho_{i}\Delta\phi} \right)\left( {\rho_{i}\sin\phi_{k}\Delta\theta} \right) = \rho_{i}^{2}\sin\phi_{k}\Delta\rho\Delta\theta\Delta\phi$$

section.paragraph: In fact, it can be shown, with the aid of the Mean Value Theorem (Exercise 51), that the volume of $$E_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ is given exactly by
$$\Delta V_{\mathit{ijk}} = {\widetilde{\rho}}_{i}^{2}\sin{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}\Delta\rho\Delta\theta\Delta\phi$$

where $$({{\widetilde{\rho}}_{i},{\widetilde{\theta}}_{j},{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}})$$ is some point in $$E_{\mathit{ijk}}$$ . Let $$({x_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast},y_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast},z_{\mathit{ijk}}^{\ast}})$$ be the rectangular coordinates of this point. Then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iiint\limits_{E}{f{({x,y,z})}}}\mathit{dV} = \lim\limits_{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}f{({x_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},y_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*},z_{\mathit{ijk}}^{*}})}\Delta V_{\mathit{ijk}}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{E}{f{({x,y,z})}}}\mathit{dV}} = \lim\limits_{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}f{({{\widetilde{\rho}}_{i}\sin{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}\cos{\widetilde{\theta}}_{j},{\widetilde{\rho}}_{i}\sin{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}\sin{\widetilde{\theta}}_{j},{\widetilde{\rho}}_{i}\cos{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}})}{\widetilde{\rho}}_{i}^{2}\sin{\widetilde{\phi}}_{k}\Delta\rho\Delta\theta\Delta\phi} \end{array}$$
But this sum is a Riemann sum for the function
$$F\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right) = f{\left( {\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\rho\cos\phi} \right)}\rho^{2}\sin\phi$$
Consequently, we have arrived at the following formula for triple integration in spherical coordinates.

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iiint\limits_{E}{f{({x,y,z})}}}\mathit{dV}} \\ {{= {\int_{c}^{d}{\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\int_{a}^{b}{f{\left( {\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\rho\cos\phi} \right)}\rho^{2}\sin\phi d\rho d\theta d\phi}}}}}} \end{array}$$
where $$E$$ is a spherical wedge given by
$$E = \left\{ \left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right) \right.{|{a \leqslant \rho \leqslant b,\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta,c \leqslant \phi \leqslant}}\left. d \right\}$$
Formula 3 says that we convert a triple integral from rectangular coordinates to spherical coordinates by writing
$${x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta} {y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta} {z = \rho\cos\phi}$$
using the appropriate limits of integration and replacing $$\mathit{dV}$$ by $$\rho^{2}\sin\phi d\rho d\theta d\phi$$ . This is illustrated in Figure 8.

section.paragraph: This formula can be extended to include more general spherical regions such as
$$E = {\{{{({\rho,\theta,\phi})}|a \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta,c \leqslant \phi \leqslant d,g_{1}{({\theta,\phi})} \leqslant \rho \leqslant g_{2}{({\theta,\phi})}}\}}$$
In this case the formula is the same as in (3) except that the limits of integration for $$\rho$$ are $$g_{1}\left( {\theta,\phi} \right)$$ and $$g_{2}\left( {\theta,\phi} \right)$$ .
Usually, spherical coordinates are used in triple integrals when surfaces such as cones and spheres form the boundary of the region of integration.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\iiint_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$B$$ is the unit ball:
Solution Since the boundary of $$B$$ is a sphere, we use spherical coordinates:
$$B = \left\{ {\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)|0 \leqslant \rho \leqslant 1,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi} \right\}$$
In addition, spherical coordinates are appropriate because
Thus (3) gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}e^{{(\rho^{2})}^{3 \slash 2}}\rho^{2}}{\sin\phi d\rho d\theta d\phi}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin\phi d\phi\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{1}\rho^{2}e^{\rho^{3}}d\rho}} \\ {\phantom{{\iiint\limits_{B}e^{{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}}}\mathit{dV}} = {\left\lbrack {- \cos\phi} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}{({2\pi})}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}e^{\rho^{3}}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{4}{3}\pi{({e - 1})}}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid that lies above the cone $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and below the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = z$$ . (See Figure 9.)

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid resembles a hemisphere mounted on an inverted cone. The cone, labeled z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), has its tip at the origin and opens upward with its circular base parallel to the x y plane and the center of the base lies on the positive z axis. The slanted side of the cone is at an angle pi/4 from the positive z axis at the origin. The hemisphere, labeled x^2 + y^2,+z^2 = z has its topmost point at (0, 0, 1), opens downward, with its rim resting on the rim of the circular base of the cone. A dashed semicircle is drawn below the hemisphere with its bottom post point at the origin.

example.paragraph: Solution Notice that the sphere passes through the origin and has center $$\left( {0,0,\frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ . We write the equation of the sphere in spherical coordinates as
$$\rho^{2} = \rho\cos\phi$$
or
$$\rho = \cos\phi$$
The equation of the cone can be written as
$$\rho\cos\phi = \sqrt{\rho^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\cos^{2}\theta + \rho^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\sin^{2}\theta} = \rho\sin\phi$$
This gives $$\sin\phi = \cos\phi$$ , or $$\phi = \pi \slash 4$$ . Therefore the description of the solid $$E$$ in spherical coordinates is
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {\rho,\theta,\phi} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi \slash 4,0 \leqslant \rho \leqslant \cos\phi} \right\}$$
Figure 10 shows how $$E$$ is swept out if we integrate first with respect to $$\rho$$ , then $$\phi$$ , and then $$\theta$$ . The volume of $$E$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {{V(E)} = {{\iiint\limits_{E}\mathit{dV}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\int_{0}^{\cos\phi}{\rho^{2}\sin\phi d\rho d\phi d\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V(E)} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\sin\phi}}\left\lbrack \frac{\rho^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = \cos\phi}d\phi}} \\ {\phantom{V(E)} = {\frac{2\pi}{3}{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{\sin\phi\cos^{3}\phi d\phi}} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\left\lbrack {- \frac{\cos^{4}\phi}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 4} = \frac{\pi}{8}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Applied Project Roller Derby
section.paragraph: Suppose that a solid ball (a marble), a hollow ball (a squash ball), a solid cylinder (a steel bar), and a hollow cylinder (a lead pipe) roll down a slope. Which of these objects reaches the bottom first? (Make a guess before proceeding.)

image.alt: Details An incline and four objects are displayed. The incline slopes upward to the right and an angle alpha from the base and has a vertical height h at its highest point. Four objects are placed at the top of the incline, on the far right. The objects are a small sphere, a large sphere, a broad pipe, and a narrow pipe, back to front.

section.paragraph: To answer this question, we consider a ball or cylinder with mass $$m$$ , radius $$r$$ , and moment of inertia $$I$$ (about the axis of rotation). If the vertical drop is $$h$$ , then the potential energy at the top is $$mgh$$ . Suppose the object reaches the bottom with velocity $$\upsilon$$ and angular velocity $$\omega$$ , so $$\upsilon = \omega r$$ . The kinetic energy at the bottom consists of two parts: $$\frac{1}{2}m\upsilon^{2}$$ from translation (moving down the slope) and $$\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$$ from rotation. If we assume that energy loss from rolling friction is negligible, then conservation of energy gives
$$mgh = \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon^{2} + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}$$

list.item: If $$y(t)$$ is the vertical distance traveled at time $$t$$ , then the same reasoning as used in Problem 1 shows that $$\upsilon^{2} = 2gy \slash \left( {1 + I^{\ast}} \right)$$ at any time $$t$$ . Use this result to show that $$y$$ satisfies the differential equation $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{dt} = \sqrt{\frac{2g}{1 + I^{\ast}}}\left( {\sin\alpha} \right)\sqrt{y}$$ where $$\alpha$$ is the angle of inclination of the plane.

By solving the differential equation in Problem 2, show that the total travel time is $$T = \sqrt{\frac{2h\left( {1 + I^{\ast}} \right)}{g\sin^{2}\alpha}}$$ This shows that the object with the smallest value of $$I^{\ast}$$ wins the race.
Show that $$I^{\ast} = \frac{1}{2}$$ for a solid cylinder and $$I^{\ast} = 1$$ for a hollow cylinder.

Calculate $$I^{\ast}$$ for a partly hollow ball with inner radius $$a$$ and outer radius $$r$$ . Express your answer in terms of $$b = a \slash r$$ . What happens as $$\left. a\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and as $$\left. a\rightarrow r \right.$$ ?

Show that $$I^{\ast} = \frac{2}{5}$$ for a solid ball and $$I^{\ast} = \frac{2}{3}$$ for a hollow ball. Thus the objects finish in the following order: solid ball, solid cylinder, hollow ball, hollow cylinder.
